claims.text: The untreated alloy is a homogenized MoNbTaTiW refractory high-entropy alloy with a balanced microstructure and standard phase distribution.
The intervention is addition of 0.5 at.% Y to MoNbTaTiW during alloy fabrication.
Conventional alloying can produce an optimal distribution of 0.5 at.% Y in the alloy matrix.
Adding 0.5 at.% Y will improve the high-temperature oxygen resistance of MoNbTaTiW.
Y addition will promote formation of a stable Al2O3 scale on MoNbTaTiW.
Protective Al2O3 scales can reduce oxidation of refractory high-entropy alloys.
The proposed oxide scale will contain finely dispersed Y2O3 particles at the oxide/alloy interface.
Yttrium will act through the reactive-element effect to enhance alumina-scale adhesion and stability.
Interfacial Y2O3 particles will reduce oxide-scale spallation.
Interfacial Y2O3 particles will stabilize the scale microstructure and retard oxygen ingress.
The Y-modified alloy will oxidize more slowly than the untreated alloy.
The Y-modified alloy will have lower oxidation mass gain than the untreated alloy.
The Y-modified alloy will exhibit better oxide-scale integrity and adhesion than the untreated alloy.
The proposed benefit will occur during exposure at 1100°C in air for 100 hours.
Nonuniform Y distribution or inadequate Y2O3 formation could limit the oxidation-resistance improvement.
Y partitioning in the complex HEA matrix and uniform interfacial Y2O3 formation are uncertain.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in mass gain relative to the Y-free control would falsify the hypothesis.
Absence of the proposed Y2O3-reinforced alumina scale or absence of improved scale adhesion would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated base alloy contains Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and W, and the only added element is Y; no Al source is specified. This conflicts with the proposed in situ formation of an Al2O3 scale and makes the intervention-to-mediator chain compositionally incoherent.
